 Business News latest economy RBI raises repo rate to 5.50% but injects ₹2.5 lakh crore: Is its policy sending mixed signals? RBI raises repo rate to 5.50% but injects ₹2.5 lakh crore: Is its policy sending mixed signals?
 The RBI’s repo rate hike to 5.50% has been accompanied by a ₹2.5 lakh crore liquidity injection, raising questions about its monetary policy direction. SBI Research warns that these moves could send mixed signals to markets and affect government bond yields.
 Join Our WhatsApp Channel Basudha Das Updated Oct 23, 2026 3:30 PM IST
 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) repo rate is 5.50%, following a 25 basis point hike during the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting in October 2026. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) decision to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% while injecting ₹2.5 lakh crore into the banking system has raised questions about the consistency of its monetary policy signals. In its latest Ecowrap report dated October 23, SBI Research flagged a potential contradiction between the central bank’s calibrated tightening stance and its liquidity operations.
 Advertisement 
 The report questioned why the RBI conducted three liquidity-injection repo operations from October 19 onwards when its policy objective was to tighten monetary conditions. SBI Research argued that the move could leave markets uncertain about whether the central bank is prioritising inflation control or liquidity support.
 Read More
 Rate hike sends a hawkish signal 
 The RBI’s October monetary policy communication was more consistent than its August messaging, according to SBI Research. The formal policy resolution, the Governor’s statement and the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) minutes conveyed a broadly aligned message on the need to address inflation risks.
 All six MPC members voted in favour of the 25-basis-point repo rate increase to 5.50%. The policy resolution adopted a hawkish tone, stating that inflation was no longer benign and that near-term policy choices were increasingly restricted to a rate hike or a pause.

 However, the committee was not unanimous on the broader policy stance. While all six members supported the rate increase, only four backed the shift to calibrated tightening. Two members preferred retaining a neutral stance.
 Against this backdrop, SBI Research questioned whether the liquidity injection was consistent with the RBI’s stated policy direction.
 Why the liquidity injection matters 
 Liquidity operations influence the amount of funds available to banks and help determine short-term money-market rates. Injecting liquidity through repo auctions provides funds to the banking system, whereas liquidity withdrawal operations work in the opposite direction.
 Advertisement 
 SBI Research noted that the RBI was pursuing calibrated liquidity tightening through measures including open market operations (OMOs) and variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) operations, while maintaining daily cash reserve requirements linked to 99% of the prescribed requirement, as described in the report.
 ALSO READ:  Rupee gains 1.9% in a week, closes at 94.71: Is RBI’s currency defence finally working? 
 The subsequent injection of ₹2.5 lakh crore, the report argued, appeared inconsistent with that approach. It raised the question of whether the RBI was moving from calibrated tightening towards a more moderate form of tightening.
 The report acknowledged that concerns about financial stability could have influenced the central bank’s actions. However, it argued that simultaneous liquidity injections and withdrawals could send conflicting signals to financial markets.
 What it means for bond investors 
 SBI Research does not expect Indian government bond yields to decline significantly, with yields at the higher end around 7.6%. It also highlighted elevated crude oil prices and the possibility of a rebound in US Treasury yields as factors that could keep domestic borrowing costs under pressure.
 The report placed the India-US yield spread at around 250 basis points and said it was moving towards normalisation.
 Advertisement 
 SBI Research recommended widening the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor, arguing that it could act as an automatic stabiliser during uncertain periods.

 What RBI MPC members said 
 In its monthly minutes, RBI Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) signalled that further rate hikes may be needed to contain inflation but cautioned against aggressive tightening that could hurt economic growth, minutes released on Wednesday showed. The RBI unanimously raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% earlier this month and shifted its stance to calibrated tightening.
 Retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September, nearing the RBI’s 6% tolerance ceiling, amid higher oil and food prices. Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta warned that additional hikes may be necessary to anchor inflation expectations, while some MPC members favoured gradual increases to protect growth.
 The RBI raised its inflation forecast for the current financial year to 5.2% from 5% and projected average inflation of 6% for October-December. While some policymakers supported pre-emptive action, others warned that rapid rate increases could weaken demand. Economists remain divided, with forecasts ranging from two to three additional hikes in the current cycle.
